d.title: Only one of the two meanings predicts a cost
d.caption: **When an engineer says “this isn't very Pythonic” they usually mean one of two very different things, and the review stalls because nobody separates them.** The useful meaning predicts something concrete: **a future reader will misread the code, or a future change will break it.** The useless meaning is **taste dressed as principle, and it produces the review comments that make people dread review.** The test is one question: **a definition of Pythonic that cannot predict a cost is a preference.**

d.title: Nineteen aphorisms, several of which contradict each other on purpose
d.caption: **`import this` is half joke, and the half that is not is load-bearing — but only if you notice the deliberate contradictions.** The pair that licenses real design work is *simple is better than complex / complex is better than complicated*: **two rungs, not one — prefer simple, and when the problem is genuinely complex, structure the complexity rather than tangling it.** And the honest reading of the famous line: **there are four ways to merge dicts and three to format a string, so read it as a design aspiration for the language rather than a claim about it.**

d.title: Idiom is compression, and the thing it compresses is attention
d.caption: **When you write `with open(path) as f:` a Python reader spends no attention on it — they know the file closes on every exit path, including the exception path, without reading further.** That is **one unit of attention freed for the part of the function that is actually specific to you.** Which is the deeper argument for idiom and the reason it is not style: **a non-idiomatic equivalent is not merely unusual, it costs every future reader a careful read of something that could have been skipped.**

d.title: Three buckets, and 95% of PEP 8's text belongs in the first
d.caption: **The automate bucket is roughly 95% of PEP 8's text and almost none of its value: indentation, quote style, line length, trailing commas, blank lines, operator spacing, import sorting — `ruff format` plus `ruff check --select I` in CI, and never discussed in review.** The decide bucket is **roughly 5% of the text and 95% of the value**, and it is where review attention belongs. And the third exists because **PEP 8 says so itself: “know when to be inconsistent”** — broken with a `noqa` and a reason.

d.title: The one layout decision a formatter cannot make for you
d.caption: **The formatter will produce something legal from any input; you decide what it has to work with** — because where a line breaks depends on **which grouping is meaningful**, and that is a fact about the code's intent rather than about its length. So the rule is to break at the seam you want the reader to see: **arguments that belong together on one line, a long boolean split so each clause is its own line, a chained call broken at the step boundaries.** A formatter run over a badly grouped line **produces a tidy version of the wrong grouping.**

d.title: A comment that says what is a liability; one that says why is the most valuable line in the file
d.caption: **A comment restating the code is a maintenance liability, because it is the part that will not be updated** — the code changes in the diff and the comment stays. The docstring rules are short and worth getting right: **imperative mood ending in a full stop — “Return the settled total”, not “Returns” and not “This function returns”.** And the two omissions matter: **do not document parameter types, because the annotations state them and cannot drift** — and **a docstring on every function regardless of value trains readers to skip docstrings.**

d.title: Most comparisons pick an example where a built-in already solves it
d.caption: **The textbook pair — `if key in d` against `try: d[key]` — is settled by `d.get()`, which is why it teaches nothing.** The interesting cases are the ones where no `get()` exists: **files, network calls, parsing, another process's state.** There the distinction is real and it is not about style: **LBYL asks whether the operation will work and then does it; EAFP does it and handles the failure** — and between the question and the action, **anything shared can change.**

d.title: EAFP is 2.2x faster on a hit and 4.4x slower on a miss
d.caption: **On the hit path EAFP wins — 0.041 against 0.089, because there is no check to pay for. On the miss path it loses badly — 0.271 against 0.062, because raising and catching an exception is expensive.** Which turns the style question into an arithmetic one: **the right choice depends on how often the operation fails, and the crossover is low — a failure rate of a few percent already favours EAFP.** So the rule is: **EAFP unless failure is the expected case.**

state: it depends on the failure rate

d.title: Five situations, and two of them have nothing to do with speed
d.caption: The two rows that are about **correctness rather than cost** are the ones to remember. **Anything about shared state — files, network, other processes — is EAFP, because a check is out of date by the time you act**, which is the race no amount of care removes. And **anything expensive or irreversible to attempt is LBYL, because it is better to check than to half-perform and roll back.** The others follow the arithmetic in §03: **rare failure favours EAFP, common failure favours LBYL.**

d.title: The same star does three different jobs depending on where it sits
d.caption: **At a call site a star spreads a sequence into positional arguments and a double star spreads a mapping into keywords** — so `f(*args)` and `f(**opts)` are the inverse of the collection 3.2 measured. The join row is the one that catches people: **`"|".join(parts)` takes an iterable, not varargs, so there is no star** — and the merge row shows the double star building a dict rather than passing one. **Three syntaxes that look the same and differ by context, which is why reading the surrounding call matters more than recognising the symbol.**

d.title: A function returning a NamedTuple unpacks and stays readable
d.caption: **`start, end = get_range()` works on anything iterable, so a plain tuple return unpacks — and a `NamedTuple` return unpacks *and* prints as `Range(start=10, end=20)`.** That is the whole argument for using one: **the call site that wants two values is unchanged, and the call site that wants one named field no longer indexes by position.** Which is 5.9's row made concrete: **a tuple return is fine until a third value is added, at which point every positional unpack is a silent reordering risk.**

d.title: A guard runs after the bindings are made, so it can use them
d.caption: **A guard runs *after* the pattern matches and its bindings exist — so it can test the values it just captured — and if the guard is false, matching continues to the next case** rather than falling out of the `match` entirely. Which gives a clean division of labour: **put structure in the pattern and values in the guard.** A pattern cannot say “a two-element list whose first element exceeds 100”; **the pattern says two-element list, the guard says exceeds 100.**

d.title: First match wins, nothing falls through, and nothing checks you covered the cases
d.caption: **Like `if`/`elif`, the first matching case wins and nothing falls through — no `break` needed — so specific patterns must come before general ones** or the general one shadows them permanently. And the absence worth planning for: **there is no exhaustiveness check at runtime.** A `match` with no matching case **does nothing and raises nothing**, so a new message type added upstream passes through silently. **A `case _:` that raises is the fix, and mypy can check exhaustiveness over an enum or a union.**

state: and mypy can check an enum

d.title: Three methods, and the rest of the sequence protocol arrives
d.caption: **Writing `__len__` and `__getitem__` and inheriting `collections.abc.Sequence` gives you `__contains__`, `__iter__`, `__reversed__`, `index` and `count`** — and the output shows all five working on a class that defined none of them. Which is 4.8's standard-library ABC argument in its clearest form: **the ABC is not there to require methods, it is there to give you implementations derived from the two you wrote.** And the derived ones are correct rather than merely present: **`__reversed__` walks backwards without building a list.**

d.title: The two-argument `iter()` is the read-until-sentinel loop
d.caption: **`iter(callable, sentinel)` calls the callable repeatedly and stops when it returns the sentinel** — which is the pre-walrus idiom for read-until-sentinel loops, and **still the cleanest when the sentinel is a specific value rather than falsiness.** The canonical use is a fixed-size read: **`iter(partial(f.read, 4096), b"")` yields chunks until the file is exhausted**, with no `while True`, no break and no repeated call written twice. And the distinction from a walrus loop is exactly that: **a walrus tests a condition, this compares against one value.**

d.title: `yield from` delegates, and the recursion flattens a tree in four lines
d.caption: **`yield from sub` yields every value the sub-generator produces, so a recursive walk needs no accumulator and no loop** — the output `['root', 'a', 'a1', 'b']` is a pre-order traversal with one statement per level. The part the equivalent `for` loop cannot do: **`yield from` also forwards `send`, `throw` and the sub-generator's return value**, so a delegating generator is transparent to its caller. **Which is why it exists at all — the loop version is equivalent only for plain iteration.**

steps.code: and it forwards send and throw

d.title: Abandoning a generator leaves the `with` inside it open
d.caption: **A `with` inside a generator releases its resource when the generator is exhausted or closed — and a generator abandoned part-way is neither.** Breaking out of a `for` over it leaves the frame suspended inside the `with`, **so the file stays open until the garbage collector finalises the generator, which on CPython is usually soon and on PyPy is not.** The fix is explicit: **wrap the consumption in `contextlib.closing`, or call `.close()`** — and the reason this is worth knowing is that **the leak is invisible in the generator's own code.**

d.title: Five tests, and three of them are about what you do next
d.caption: **The first row is the one people quote and the middle three are the ones that actually decide it**, because they are about consumption rather than size. **You consume it once, you only iterate, early exit is likely** — all three favour a generator and none of them mention how big the data is. And the last row is the sharpest: **you cannot sort or reverse a generator without materialising it**, so a pipeline that ends in `sorted()` has already paid for the list and should probably have been one.

d.title: A bare `return True` swallows KeyboardInterrupt and your own bugs
d.caption: **Returning `True` from `__exit__` suppresses *every* exception — including `KeyboardInterrupt` and bugs in your own code — and the measured output is the whole problem: `execution continues, and nothing was logged`.** So if suppression is genuinely wanted, **name what you are ignoring: `contextlib.suppress(FileNotFoundError)` is fine precisely because it says which exception.** Which is 5.1's Zen row doing real work: **errors should never pass silently, unless *explicitly* silenced** — and the explicitness is the exception type.

d.title: `with a, b, c:` needs the count at write time; ExitStack does not
d.caption: **`with a, b, c:` works when you know the resources at write time. When the number varies at runtime, `ExitStack` manages them and unwinds in reverse order** — so opening N files from a list is a loop of `stack.enter_context(...)` and every one closes, including on an exception part-way through the loop. The two uses worth knowing beyond that: **`callback()` registers arbitrary cleanup without a context manager, and `pop_all()` transfers ownership out** — which is how a factory returns a half-built object without leaking on failure.

d.title: A missing key is 0, and the arithmetic operators are the reason to use it
d.caption: **`Counter` returns `0` for a missing key rather than raising**, which removes the `if key in counts` from every increment. And `most_common(2)` answers the question people write a sort for. The rows worth knowing are the last three: **`+` merges and sums, `-` subtracts and drops anything that reaches zero or below, and `&` keeps the minimum of each key** — so a diff between two days' counts is one operator, and **the asymmetry of `-` is deliberate: a `Counter` of counts has no meaning below zero.**

d.title: Four record types, and the choice is whether tuple behaviour is wanted
d.caption: **A `NamedTuple` unpacks like a tuple *and* reads by name — `OrderLine(sku='W-1', quantity=3, ...)` prints usefully and `line.sku` works** — so it is right for multi-value returns, coordinates and database rows. **A frozen dataclass is usually clearer when tuple behaviour is not wanted, and it supports `slots`.** The row that is easy to get wrong is the last: **a dict is right when the keys are data rather than a fixed schema** — and reaching for a record type there means inventing a schema the data does not have.

d.title: ChainMap searches the layers and never copies them
d.caption: **A `ChainMap` searches its mappings left to right, so the first layer wins — `debug` is `True` from the override, `timeout` is 10 from the middle layer, `retries` is 3 from the defaults** — and nothing was merged. Which is the difference from 2.3's spread: **a merge produces a snapshot and a `ChainMap` stays live, so a later change to the defaults is visible immediately.** And the `.maps` attribute is the reason it is good for configuration: **you can see which layer every value came from**, which a merged dict has permanently lost.

d.title: The same pipeline gives 21 the first time and nothing the second
d.caption: **Every `itertools` callable returns an iterator, not a list — nothing is computed until you iterate, and once you have iterated, it is spent.** Which is what lets you **chain ten transformations over a 40 GB file with constant memory**, and what makes **a pipeline that works in the REPL return nothing on the second use.** The measured sequence is the whole lesson: **21, then 0, then `[]`** — and the fix when you need it twice is `itertools.tee` or a list, **both of which give up the memory property you came for.**

d.title: Five reshapings, and the last one is a grouping with a catch
d.caption: **`chain` concatenates, `islice` slices an iterator without materialising it, `batched` chunks with a short final batch, `compress` selects by a parallel mask of booleans.** The last row is `groupby`, and its behaviour is the one that surprises: **it groups *consecutive* equal keys, so it finds `['data-1', '# not-a-header', 'data-2']` as three groups rather than two** — because the input was not sorted. **`groupby` without a prior `sorted` on the same key is almost always a bug**, and it is a quiet one.

d.title: It works, it was written in an afternoon, and everyone is slightly afraid of it
d.caption: **This runs nightly: it reads the day's orders, applies volume discounts, writes a summary file and emails anyone over their credit limit.** The description is the point — **four responsibilities, one file, no arguments and no tests** — and none of that is visible as a bug, which is why nobody has touched it. **The three passes that follow separate the three different kinds of problem: what is wrong, what cannot be tested, and what will fail at 3am** — and they are deliberately not done at once.

d.title: Six correctness fixes, and two of them were invisible on CPython
d.caption: **`Decimal(r[2])` rather than `float` — because `0.1 + 0.2` is not `0.3` in binary floating point, and eighteen months of accumulating that is why the report never quite reconciles.** Two were hidden by the implementation: **the original leaked a handle on every exception and never closed the writer if a row raised, which CPython's refcounting hides and PyPy does not.** And one was hidden by the data: **dicts preserve insertion order, so two identical days produced diffable-looking files that differed everywhere** until `sorted` was added.

d.title: Two tests in 0.01s, which is what the seams bought
d.caption: **`2 passed in 0.01s` — and the measurement that matters is the time, not the count.** The pass did not add tests to the script; **it separated the pure calculation from the I/O so that a test needs no file, no SMTP server and no clock.** Which is the general shape: **a function that reads, computes and writes can only be tested by providing all three, so the seam goes between computing and the rest.** And the discount rule is now testable **in isolation, at every boundary value, in milliseconds.**

d.title: Seven production changes, and four of them are about the next failure
d.caption: **A date argument, because any job derived from `date.today()` cannot be re-run or backfilled without editing the source.** Then three that are about what a crash leaves behind: **dated filenames, because `summary.txt` was overwritten every night including when today's was wrong; write-then-rename, because a crash mid-write leaves a truncated report that looks complete; and distinct exit codes, so a scheduler can retry a 2 in an hour, page on a 3, and merely log a 1.** And the quality gate: **silently skipping rows is right for a handful and wrong for a third of the file.**
